cards.title: Input schema, output schema, and the *scratch* in between.
cards.body: `StateGraph` takes one full state plus optional `input_schema` and `output_schema`. Callers only pass input keys and only get output keys back; scratch fields stay inside the graph. Same dict, three views.
cards.why: Interview question: 'how do you stop internal fields leaking to the API response?' — this is the answer, not a post-filter.

code.src:
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END

class In(TypedDict): question: str
class Out(TypedDict): answer: str
class State(In, Out): scratch: str          # full state = in + out + private

def solve(s: State): return {"scratch": "notes", "answer": s["question"].upper()}

g = StateGraph(State, input_schema=In, output_schema=Out)
g.add_node("solve", solve); g.add_edge(START, "solve"); g.add_edge("solve", END)
print(g.compile().invoke({"question": "hi"}))   # {'answer': 'HI'} — no scratch

cards.title: Time travel = pick a *checkpoint_id*, not just a thread_id.
cards.body: Every checkpoint on a thread has its own id. `graph.get_state_history(config)` lists them newest-first. Passing a specific `checkpoint_id` in `configurable` makes the next call branch from that point instead of the latest one.

quiz.question: Step 3 of a 5-step run used a bad search query. You want to rerun from *before* step 3 with a corrected query, keeping steps 1–2. What do you do?
options: Clear the thread and invoke again with the fixed query
Find the checkpoint before step 3 in get_state_history, call update_state with that checkpoint_id and the new query, then invoke(None, cfg)
Edit the SQLite checkpoint row by hand
Set recursion_limit=3 so it stops early
quiz.explain: update_state against an older checkpoint creates a *fork*: a new checkpoint whose parent is the one you chose. invoke(None, cfg) then resumes from the fork. Steps 1–2 are never recomputed, and the original branch is still there for comparison.

cards.title: No reducer + two parallel writers = an error, not a merge.
cards.body: Without a reducer a key is *overwritten*. When two nodes in the same superstep both return that key, LangGraph has no rule for which wins and refuses rather than guess.

quiz.question: Nodes `a` and `b` run in parallel after START and both return `{"result": ...}`. `result: str` has no reducer. What happens?
options: The later node silently wins
Both values are concatenated
InvalidUpdateError: can receive only one value per step
The graph deadlocks
quiz.explain: LangGraph raises InvalidUpdateError at runtime. The fix is to declare how writes combine: `Annotated[list[str], operator.add]` to collect both, or a custom reducer that keeps the best. Reducers are not optional once you fan out.

cards.title: Give the Store an embedder and `search()` becomes semantic.
cards.body: `InMemoryStore(index={"embed": embeddings, "dims": 1536})` indexes every `put()` value. `store.search(("users", uid), query="food preferences", limit=3)` then returns the nearest memories, not just key lookups. Postgres store does the same with pgvector.
cards.why: This is how a 'remember what the user likes' feature works without stuffing every memory into the prompt.

cards.title: RRF in eight lines — no scores compared, only ranks.
cards.body: Reciprocal Rank Fusion gives each doc `1/(k+rank)` from every list it appears in and sums. BM25 scores and cosine scores never meet, so the scale mismatch disappears. k≈60 flattens the top ranks so one list cannot dominate.
cards.why: Interviewers love 'how do you merge BM25 and vector results?' — writing RRF from memory ends the question.

cards.title: `include_raw=True` turns a crash into a value you can inspect.
cards.body: By default `with_structured_output` raises when the model's JSON fails Pydantic validation. With `include_raw=True` it returns `{"raw", "parsed", "parsing_error"}` so you decide what to do.

quiz.question: 1 in 200 calls, the model emits a status outside your Enum and the whole request 500s. Cheapest robust fix?
options: Wrap the call in try/except and return None
Use with_structured_output(Schema, include_raw=True) and route parsing_error cases to a retry with the error text appended
Switch the Enum to str
Increase temperature so it explores more
quiz.explain: include_raw gives you the raw AIMessage *and* the validation error. Feeding that error back ('status must be one of …') fixes most cases in one retry. Loosening the schema hides the bug; a bare except loses the information you need to recover.

cards.title: `.with_retry()` and `.batch()` are free on every Runnable.
cards.body: Because a chain is a Runnable, resilience and throughput are methods, not rewrites. `with_retry` wraps one step with exponential backoff; `batch` runs inputs concurrently under `max_concurrency`.
cards.why: Same chain, zero new code, 5× faster offline eval runs.

code.src:
chain = prompt | llm.with_retry(stop_after_attempt=3) | parser

answers = chain.batch(
    [{"q": "What is RRF?"}, {"q": "What is a reducer?"}],
    config={"max_concurrency": 5},
)

cards.title: A trace is a *tree* of spans, and each span has a type.
cards.body: The root span is the agent call. Children are typed: `RETRIEVER`, `LLM`, `TOOL`, `CHAIN`. The type is what lets the MLflow UI render retrieved docs as docs and tool calls as calls, and what evaluators like `RetrievalGroundedness` look for.
cards.why: If your custom span has the wrong type, retrieval evaluators silently find no context.

diagram.caption: Set span_type explicitly on @mlflow.trace when autolog can't infer it.

cards.title: `Command(goto=...)` lets a node route *and* update in one return.
cards.body: Instead of a node plus a separate conditional edge, the supervisor returns a `Command`. The `Literal` in the return type tells LangGraph which destinations exist so the graph still draws correctly.
cards.why: Cleaner than add_conditional_edges when the decision and the state update belong together.

cards.title: DeepEval faithfulness: does the answer stay inside the retrieved context?
cards.body: An `LLMTestCase` carries input, actual output and the retrieved chunks. `FaithfulnessMetric` extracts claims from the answer and checks each against the context. `.reason` tells you *which* claim was unsupported.
cards.why: Put the `.reason` in your CI log — a score alone never tells you what to fix.

code.src:
from deepeval.metrics import FaithfulnessMetric
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase

tc = LLMTestCase(input=q, actual_output=answer, retrieval_context=chunks)
metric = FaithfulnessMetric(threshold=0.8)
metric.measure(tc)
print(metric.score, metric.reason)

cards.title: One context manager counts tokens across *every* model call inside it.
cards.body: `get_usage_metadata_callback()` from `langchain_core.callbacks` yields a handler whose `.usage_metadata` sums input/output tokens per model name for everything invoked inside the `with` block — chains, agents, nested calls.
cards.why: Multiply by your price table at the end and you have cost-per-request without touching the agent code.

cards.title: `GraphRecursionError` at 25 — what is being counted?
cards.body: LangGraph stops a run after `recursion_limit` supersteps (default 25). A superstep is one round of node execution; in a ReAct loop that is model → tools → model, so 25 supersteps ≈ 12 tool rounds.

quiz.question: Your agent raises GraphRecursionError. Which number did it exceed?
options: 25 tool calls
25 supersteps (rounds of node execution)
25 messages in state
25 000 tokens
quiz.explain: Supersteps, not tool calls or tokens. Raise it with config={"recursion_limit": 50} for legitimately long tasks, but first ask whether the loop is stuck — a stuck agent that gets 50 steps just costs twice as much.

cards.title: A subgraph shares state through *overlapping keys* — nothing else crosses the wall.
cards.body: When parent and child state schemas share a key (say `messages`), the child reads and writes it directly. Keys only the child has stay private. If the schemas share nothing, wrap the child in a function that translates in and out.
cards.why: This is how teams own separate graphs and still compose them.

cards.title: Ask for two stream modes and you get `(mode, chunk)` tuples.
cards.body: Passing a list to `stream_mode` multiplexes: `messages` yields `(token, metadata)` as the model generates; `updates` yields a dict per finished node. One loop drives both the live text and the progress bar.
cards.why: `metadata["langgraph_node"]` tells the UI which node is talking.

cards.title: Summarise, then wipe: the two-write pattern for long chats.
cards.body: A summary node returns `{"summary": text, "messages": [RemoveMessage(id=REMOVE_ALL_MESSAGES), HumanMessage(text)]}`. The reducer clears the list first, then appends the summary as the new first message. Order inside the list matters.
cards.why: Without the wipe your context grows forever; without re-inserting the summary the agent forgets everything.

cards.title: `finish_reason == "length"` means the JSON you got is *cut off*.
cards.body: The standardised finish reason tells you *why* generation stopped: `stop` (natural), `length` (hit max_tokens), `tool_calls`, `content_filter`. On structured output, `length` almost always means truncated JSON.

quiz.question: A with_structured_output call fails to parse, and finish_reason is "length". Best next step?
options: Retry the identical call — it's random
Raise max_tokens (or shrink the schema) and retry
Lower temperature
Switch to include_raw=False
quiz.explain: The model ran out of output budget mid-object. Retrying unchanged will hit the same wall. Give it more tokens or ask for less. Checking finish_reason *before* parsing turns a confusing parse error into an obvious one.

cards.title: Register a scorer, start it with a sample rate — it then grades live traces.
cards.body: In MLflow 3.x a `@scorer` function can be registered to an experiment and started with a `ScorerSamplingConfig`. From then on MLflow runs it on a fraction of new traces and attaches the result as feedback, without you calling evaluate().
cards.why: Offline evals catch regressions before deploy; online scorers catch the ones that only show up in real traffic.

code.src:
import mlflow
from mlflow.genai.scorers import scorer, ScorerSamplingConfig

@scorer
def quotes_price(outputs):              # cheap, deterministic check
    return "£" in str(outputs)

mlflow.set_experiment("support-agent")
quotes_price.register(name="quotes_price")
quotes_price.start(sampling_config=ScorerSamplingConfig(sample_rate=0.2))

cards.title: A rejected tool call *still* needs a ToolMessage — so LangChain fakes one and tags it.
cards.body: Provider APIs require one ToolMessage per `tool_call_id` or the next model call errors. When a human rejects a call in HITL middleware, LangChain inserts a synthetic ToolMessage saying it was rejected, and since langchain 1.5.2 tags it with source metadata so traces and evals can tell human rejections from real tool output.
cards.why: Filter on that tag when building eval datasets, or your 'tool results' will include things no tool ever said.

cards.title: `InjectedState` gives a tool graph state the model never sees.
cards.body: An argument annotated with `InjectedState` is stripped from the schema sent to the model and filled from the current state at call time. Since langgraph 1.2.23, tools dispatched through `Send` see the same state as ones on normal edges.
cards.why: User id, tenant, auth token: things a tool needs but the model must never be able to choose.

cards.title: Routing by difficulty is now a middleware, not a hand-rolled node.
cards.body: langchain 1.5.0 added `ModelRouterMiddleware` (beta) to `create_agent`: a router function inspects the request and returns which model to use for that turn, so the cheap/expensive split from the routing card lives in one pluggable place. Beta means the signature may still move — check the docs before relying on it.
cards.why: Same idea as the tiny-classifier router, but the agent loop stays untouched.

cards.title: A retried stream *starts over* — your consumer must expect that.
cards.body: With langchain-openai 1.8.4+ a 5xx mid-stream is retried under `max_retries`. The retry re-generates from the beginning, so tokens you already showed may be sent again. Buffer per attempt, or reset the UI when a new stream starts.
cards.why: Retry is only safe when the consumer is idempotent — same rule as any queue.

code.src:
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-5-mini", max_retries=3)
buf = []
for chunk in llm.stream("Explain RRF in three lines"):
    buf.append(chunk.content)            # commit to the UI only when done
text = "".join(buf)

cards.title: Feedback is the bridge from *traces* to *datasets*.
cards.body: A feedback score on a run (from the CLI, the SDK, or a user thumbs-down) is a filterable field. `runs where feedback.correctness < 0.5` is a saved query, and 'add these runs to dataset' is one click. Bad production runs become tomorrow's regression tests.
cards.why: Interview framing: trace → feedback → dataset → eval is the loop; feedback is the join key.

cards.title: `durability=` trades crash-safety for speed, per call.
cards.body: `exit` writes one checkpoint at the end (fastest); `async` writes after each step without waiting (default); `sync` waits for each write before the next step (safest). Same graph, three risk profiles.
cards.why: Batch backfills want `exit`; anything with a human waiting on a resume wants `sync`.

code.src:
cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1"}}

graph.invoke(inputs, cfg, durability="exit")    # one write at the end
graph.invoke(inputs, cfg, durability="async")   # default: write after each step
graph.invoke(inputs, cfg, durability="sync")    # wait for each write

cards.title: Retry at the *node*, not inside the function.
cards.body: `add_node(..., retry_policy=RetryPolicy(...))` retries that node with backoff on the exceptions you name. The node body stays clean, and the retry shows up as repeated attempts in the trace instead of a hidden loop.
cards.why: Only retry on transient errors (timeouts, 5xx); retrying a ValueError just burns money.

code.src:
import httpx
from langgraph.types import RetryPolicy

builder.add_node(
    "fetch", fetch_node,
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(
        max_attempts=3, initial_interval=0.5, backoff_factor=2.0,
        retry_on=httpx.HTTPStatusError,
    ),
)

cards.title: Proactive agents run on *events and schedules*, not on chat turns.
cards.body: LangChain's write-up on building proactive agents names three triggers (real-world events, developer schedules, agent-set schedules) and three memory signals (seed, feedback, outcome). A background 'dreaming' job updates memory from recent traces. Over 70% of runs on Managed Deep Agents now start from a schedule.
cards.why: The hard parts they list — salience, expiry, duplication — are memory problems, not prompting problems. This feed is itself a scheduled agent.

cards.title: Hide the payload, keep the shape: new LangSmith trace privacy controls.
cards.body: Three Enterprise controls landed on 17 Nov: hide trace inputs/outputs while keeping the run tree, latency and cost; user groups with per-workspace permissions; and trace-level ABAC policies keyed on root-run metadata such as customer id.

quiz.question: Your on-call engineers must debug slow agent runs but must never read customer messages. Which control fits?
options: Delete traces after 24h
Hide inputs/outputs while keeping the run tree, latency and cost visible
Give on-call read access to one workspace only
Turn tracing off in production
quiz.explain: Latency debugging needs the span tree and timings, not the text. Hiding payloads keeps exactly that. Workspace scoping controls *which* traces, not *which fields*; deleting or disabling throws away the signal you need.

cards.title: Cost per *merged PR*: LangSmith 'outcomes' tie agent threads to results.
cards.body: Public beta on LangSmith Cloud (18 Nov): an outcome links a GitHub PR or GitLab MR to the coding-agent threads that produced it. Spend is split by PR state (open/closed/merged) and 'unattributed', and threads are labelled by work type. Supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot and Deep Agents.
cards.why: Token cost per request is an engineering metric; cost per shipped change is the one a manager asks for.

cards.title: Tool Gateway: one MCP URL, policies in the middle, every call traced.
cards.body: Public beta (19 Nov). A 'tool kit' is exposed at a single URL (with a search mode for big kits). Each call runs as the user (OAuth on first use) or as the agent (profiles). Deny and approval policies sit in front; the audit log is Enterprise-only.
cards.why: This is guardrails-as-infrastructure: the deny policy lives outside the prompt, so the model cannot talk its way past it.

diagram.caption: Built-in servers: Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, GitHub, Linear.

cards.title: Preventive vs detective: two halves of agent governance.
cards.body: LangChain's governance post splits controls into *preventive* (runtime guardrails, pre-production evals) and *detective* (online evals, alerts, drift detection). Their number: across 16,000+ production agents, 87% of teams had tracing in place before first deploy.
cards.why: Map your own stack: guardrail nodes and CI evals are preventive; online scorers and LangSmith alerts are detective. Most teams only have the first half.

cards.title: A 'knowledge factory': agents flag gaps, a curator agent fixes the store.
cards.body: Harrison Chase's post (21 Nov) describes three kinds of knowledge — skills, domain knowledge, data-access guidance — and a loop: working agents call a tool to flag missing or wrong knowledge; a scheduled curator agent reads the flags, raw sources (Notion, Slack) and traces, then updates the store (skill files in GitHub or LangSmith Context Hub).
cards.why: Memory for one user is the Store. Knowledge for all agents is this loop.
